extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and medical/psychological professionals (readers of Popular Science Monthly)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying causes, character, clinical significance, prevention, and (limited) treatment of hallucinations; includes criteria for when hallucinations indicate insanity versus when they may occur in otherwise sane persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin by downward action of idea upon sense (imagination-induced hallucination)
rubrics_metrics.description: One way in which hallucination is produced — by the downward action of idea upon sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by examples from sane minds (Blake, Shakespeare): intense imagination or dominant ideas may 'call up images' that become externally perceived; persistent exercise of this power may threaten mental stability (painter who painted 300 portraits then lost his senses). In such cases the senses become 'enslaved by the dominant idea' and work only in its service, producing misinterpretation of innocent gestures and words as evidence of a conspiracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin in the sensory organ or sensory ganglion (bodily causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stimulation of the organ or of its ganglion will undoubtedly give rise to hallucination: a blow on the eye makes a person see sparks..., any organ of sense when irritated either by direct stimulus or by a perverted state of the blood will have the same sensation aroused in it as by its natural stimulus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: belladonna causes staring and grasping at imaginary objects; injected alcohol in dogs produces vivid hallucinations. Fevers and bodily diseases often proceed from disorder of the sensory centres (see Nicolai case). Such hallucinations may not affect judgment and can sometimes be relieved by addressing bodily cause (e.g., bloodletting relieved Nicolai).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustion, fatigue, starvation, or disease as causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhaustion of the nerve-centres by excessive fatigue, mental and bodily, or by starvation, or by disease, will cause a person to see visions sometimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical and literary examples (Brutus, religious ascetics, shipwrecked sailors, dying persons) show how extreme physical exhaustion or prolonged fasting/asceticism produces visions that reflect mood (angels or devils) and may drive dangerous acts (e.g., throwing oneself overboard to reach imagined fields).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epileptic hallucinations often precede unconscious fits (possible origin of prophetic visions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A vivid hallucination of one or other of the senses frequently precedes the unconsciousness of an epileptic fit — a command or threat in a distinct voice, a figure, or a flash/halo of bright light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such sensory-centre-origin hallucinations (not produced by prior thought) can be interpreted as miraculous or prophetic (example: epileptic laborer who claimed the Holy Ghost; discussion of Mohammed). They commonly leave vivid memory and strong impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed origin of hallucinations (interaction of thought and sense centres)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although they sometimes originate primarily in the sensory centres, and sometimes primarily in the higher centres of thought, it is very probable that, in many instances, they have a mixed origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of intimate structural and functional connection between centres of thought and sense, closely connected centres are likely to sympathize in suffering; many hallucinations therefore arise from combined causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hallucinations reflect the dominant morbid feelings and ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: In each case the hallucinations reflect the dominant morbid feelings and ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: general paralysis with elation leads to delusions of wealth/grandeur and hoarding worthless objects as jewels; melancholia leads to gloomy delusions, seeing devils, hearing jeers. The content of hallucinations is shaped by the patient's underlying mood and ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for sanity: awareness of the hallucination's true nature
rubrics_metrics.description: No one pretends that a person who, laboring under hallucinations, knows their true nature, as Nicolai did, is insane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the hallucination is the consistent expression of an earnest and coherent belief which is not itself the product of insanity, it is no proof of insanity, though it may indicate brain instability. A person may observe, reason about, and distinguish such apparitions from reality (Nicolai's case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for insanity: hallucinations inconsistent with common-sense and governing conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person has hallucinations that are utterly inconsistent with the observation and common-sense of the rest of mankind; when he cannot correct the mistakes of one sense by the evidence of another; when he believes in them in spite of confuting evidence, and when he suffers them to govern his conduct, then he must certainly be accounted insane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such persons are out of harmony with others, unpredictable, and may be dangerous: persecutory delusions, voices commanding self-harm or murder, public nuisances (appealing to magistrates), and attacks on supposed persecutors are cited as consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acute versus chronic hallucinations: prognosis and treatment prospects
rubrics_metrics.description: When once they have taken firm hold of a person, they are seldom got rid of. When they occur during an acute case of insanity they often disappear as the excitement passes off, or soon afterward, but when they have become chronic they hold their ground in defiance of every kind of assault upon them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many attempts to prove the hallucination false by every possible device have failed. Acute, medically-caused hallucinations (e.g., delirium of fever) may remit with resolution of physical illness; chronic hallucinations are very resistant to correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention by maintaining bodily health
rubrics_metrics.description: It is of the first importance ... to keep the body in good health; for not only will bodily disorder directly occasion hallucinations by disturbance of the sensory centres, but by its depressing influence on the entire nervous system it hinders sound, and predisposes to unsound, thought and feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical counsel: watchfully keep the body healthy — a sound body is the foundation of a sound mind; neglect of the body predisposes to hallucination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention by mental cultivation and close converse with nature and humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: The closest, most exact, and sincere converse with nature, physical and human ... Habitual contact with realities in thought and deed is a strong defense against illusions of all sorts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: thoroughness and sincerity of observation; avoid speculative meditations and solitary brooding; live and work among men; inform the mind with true perceptions so there is no room for false perceptions; balanced faculties prevent exaggeration and delusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hallucinations of bodily disease may leave judgment intact (diagnostic pointer)
rubrics_metrics.description: The hallucinations which occur in fevers and in some other bodily diseases evidently proceed directly from disorder of the sensory centres, and not from the action of morbid idea upon sense; for, we have seen that before they are fixed the intellect struggles against them successfully and holds them in check.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic implication: if a patient can observe and reason about apparitions and distinguishes them from reality (as Nicolai), a bodily sensory-centre origin is likely; treating the bodily cause may relieve hallucinations (e.g., bloodletting in Nicolai's case).
